meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'How Will You Get Robots to Pay Union Dues?" "How Will You Get Robots to Buy Cars?'?
meta.ogDescription: Walter Reuther told this story about himself from 1954 on. Henry Ford II was added later: Reuther only ever said “a company official.”

answer.label: Not Henry Ford II — the exchange is Walter Reuther’s
answer.authorDates: 1907–1970 · President of the United Automobile Workers
answer.sourceLine: Reuther told this story about himself repeatedly from 1954 onward, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes he is its source. In every version he gave, the man who needled him is an unnamed “company official” or “one of the management people” at Ford’s automated engine plant in Cleveland — never Henry Ford II. QI “was unable to find any persuasive evidence that Reuther was speaking with Henry Ford II,” and calls the Ford II casting a later embellishment. The tidy “robots…union dues…buy cars” phrasing is a modern polish, too: Reuther’s own words were looser and varied every time he told it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Automation: A Report to the UAW-CIO Economic and Collective Bargaining Conference
January 1955, p. 6, under the heading “Parable” — reporting a conference held 12–13 November 1954
Ford’s automated engine plant, Cleveland, Ohio
An unnamed company official — not Henry Ford II

source.excerpt: A company official proudly pointed to some new automatically controlled machines and asked Reuther: “How are you going to collect union dues from these guys?” Reuther replied: “How are you going to get them to buy Fords?”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest evidence as the UAW-CIO’s report Automation (January 1955), p. 6, where the exchange runs between Reuther and “a company official.”

Reuther’s own account, in a November 1956 address to a National Education Association council, describes “one of the management people, with a slightly gleeful tone in his voice” asking how he would collect union dues from the machines — and his reply that what troubled him was “how to sell automobiles to these machines.” QI cites the speech from Walter P. Reuther: Selected Papers (Macmillan, 1961), p. 180.

He repeated it under oath. In January 1958 Senate testimony, QI records, Reuther said “they said to me, ‘Aren’t you worried about how you are going to collect union dues from all of these machines?’” — still no named executive, and the wording altered again.

QI ↗ states plainly that it “was unable to find any persuasive evidence that Reuther was speaking with Henry Ford II,” and dates an early Ford II telling to a Canadian newspaper in 1979. Contemporary reports were sceptical from the start: a Connecticut paper called it “legendary” in November 1954, and Time filed it under automation’s “folklore” in March 1956.
source.excerptNote: The earliest printed form of the exchange, from the UAW-CIO’s own January 1955 conference report, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Note what it does not contain: robots, and Henry Ford II.
source.rightsHolder: The UAW (the 1955 conference report) and Macmillan / the Walter P. Reuther estate (the 1961 Selected Papers)
source.rightsNote: Both documented sources — the UAW-CIO report of 1955 and Walter P. Reuther: Selected Papers of 1961 — were first published well after 1931, so quotle.info treats the wording as in copyright and quotes only what is needed to establish it.

author.name: Walter Reuther
author.heading: About Walter Reuther
author.metaLine: 1907–1970 · American labour leader · President of the United Automobile Workers
author.bio: Walter Philip Reuther built the United Automobile Workers into one of the most powerful unions in the United States and was a prominent figure in the civil rights movement. Automation was his defining preoccupation in the 1950s, and he argued the case in speeches, at union conferences and in Senate testimony — which is where this exchange comes from, and why it exists in half a dozen slightly different wordings, all of them his.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two separate errors travel together here: the wrong sparring partner, and a set of words nobody actually spoke.

items.why: Reuther never named him. QI ↗ could find no persuasive evidence Ford II was present and calls the casting “a later embellishment added by some intermediate storyteller.” Its earliest example of that version is a 1979 newspaper column — against the January 1955 report that printed the exchange with no Ford II in it.

The 1955 text says “automatically controlled machines” and “these guys”; Reuther’s own 1956 and 1958 versions say “machines.” The snappy robot phrasing belongs to later retellings, per QI’s chronology ↗.
The retort really is his, in substance and by his own repeated account — though he never told it twice in quite the same words. QI ↗ concludes he is the source of the anecdote.

items.scope: Called a legend from the beginning
items.why: A Connecticut newspaper ran it in November 1954 as “one of those legendary stories that may not be true,” and Time in March 1956 called it one of automation’s “most widely told legends” — both per QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Reuther really made the joke. He made it to a Ford man whose name nobody recorded — and the version with Henry Ford II in it was assembled decades later, by people retelling a story they liked.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Reuther was not scoring a debating point. He told this story at an automation conference, to educators, and to a Senate antitrust subcommittee, because it compressed the argument he spent the 1950s making: that a factory which needs no workers also faces a country with no wages, and that the industry celebrating its new machines had not thought about who would buy what they made.

That is why the anecdote keeps resurfacing whenever automation does — it was quoted back into circulation by The Economist in 2011, which is what prompted Quote Investigator to check it in the first place.
detailsBody: The embellishment is instructive about how quotations decay. An anonymous “company official” is a weak character, so storytellers upgraded him to the man whose name was on the building. Nothing about the exchange’s meaning changes — which is exactly why nobody checked. The version that survives is the one that tells better, and it took a specialist re-reading the 1955 conference report to notice that the best-known detail in it was never there.
context.pull: You can make automobiles, but consumers are still made in the good old fashioned way.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest evidence is the January 1955 UAW-CIO report 'Automation', page 6, under the heading 'Parable', where a 'company official' asks Reuther 'How are you going to collect union dues from these guys?' and Reuther replies 'How are you going to get them to buy Fords?'

QI states it 'was unable to find any persuasive evidence that Reuther was speaking with Henry Ford II' and calls the Ford II version 'a later embellishment added by some intermediate storyteller', its earliest example being a 1979 Calgary Herald item.

QI quotes Reuther's November 1956 NEA address (published in Walter P. Reuther: Selected Papers, Macmillan, 1961, p. 180) referring to 'one of the management people' and his reply about 'how to sell automobiles to these machines', and his January 1958 Senate testimony with a further variant wording.
QI records a Connecticut newspaper calling the story 'legendary' on 28 November 1954 and Time magazine calling it one of automation's 'most widely told legends' in March 1956.
Walter Philip Reuther lived 1 September 1907 to 9 May 1970 and built the United Automobile Workers.
Henry Ford II lived 4 September 1917 to 29 September 1987.
